item.title: [World news | The Guardian] Monday briefing: You asked, we answered – how will the US midterms go?
item.description:
In today’s newsletter: As Americans get ready to vote on whether the Republican party remains in control of Congress, our Washington editor talks about the disconnect between Trump and his supporters

Good morning. Later today, Donald Trump will be in the state of Nebraska to rev up supporters as he kicks off a campaign blitz of rallies ahead of the midterm elections on 3 November.

If his early speeches are anything to go by, cornhuskers can anticipate poll denial, accusations of veganism and an expletive ratio that my nine-year-old would love. And Nebraskans may love it, too: aside from one “blue dot” district in Omaha, Republicans argue their support is steady in the state that has easily backed Trump three times.

UK politics | The Greens in England and Wales have formally adopted a policy that equates Zionism with racism and calls for Israel to be replaced by a single Palestinian state.

Schools | Lawyers and campaigners have condemned the “horrifying” scale of child-on-child sexual abuse in schools after a Guardian investigation revealed thousands of sexual offences against under-13s are reported to police each year.

Brazil | Brazil’s presidential race will go to a second round after the far-right candidate, Flávio Bolsonaro, beat the incumbent leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, but failed to secure the outright majority he needed to avoid a runoff.

Environment | A study of Europe’s summer paints a grim picture for the future, with doctors and climate scientists calling on governments to stop burning fossil fuels, shade buildings, green cities, and install air conditioning in hospitals, schools and care homes.

US military | The US Air Force has pulled its bombers from RAF Fairford following an investigation into an alleged planned terror attack at the base.

Tuesday | ABC News is suing the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) over its licence review, and on Thursday its hearing will take place. The broadcaster claims the review, ordered by Donald Trump in April over comedian Jimmy Kimmel’s comments about the US president, is a “retaliatory campaign” in violation of its first amendment rights.

Wednesday | Kemi Badenoch is to speak at the Conservative party conference in Birmingham. This day also marks the third anniversary of the 7 October attacks by Hamas. In London, the Met are asking organisers of a pro-Palestinian student march to move the event.

Thursday | Holborn and St Pancras will hold its byelection. The seat belongs to former prime minister and Labour party leader Keir Starmer, who held it from 2015 until his resignation in September.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] 'We're waiting to sweep up their votes': Three days inside the Green Party conference
item.description:
'We're waiting to sweep up their votes': Three days inside the Green Party conference

Submitted by Imran Mulla on Sun, 10/04/2026 - 11:29
The Brighton conference revealed a party riding a wave of support but wrestling with internal tensions, political strategy and how to make an impact in Burnham's Britain

When I sat down with Mothin Ali early on Sunday, he was in an energetic mood.

It was the third and final day of what must have been an arduous Green Party conference for its co-deputy leader, who was dressed in his usual suit and flat cap. 

"It's been a fantastic year," Ali beamed. "We had 400 councillors elected in May, 1,300 councillors in all, a fifth MP in parliament and our membership has quadrupled.

"It's a phenomenal record so far."

The Greens surged in the polls last year after Polanski was elected leader. They gained further momentum and credibility with a by-election victory in Gorton and Denton in February and then took more votes from Labour in the May local elections than Reform did. 

Polanski is at least partially responsible for Keir Starmer's downfall and Andy Burnham's premiership. On Friday evening the renowned political analyst John Curtice argued as much at a packed fringe event.

The conference in the sunny seaside town of Brighton was full of energy. For many members it was the event of the year: friends roved the conference in groups and went off to restaurants and bars in the evening. They were diverse in age and ethnicity; many wore keffiyehs and Palestine badges. 

But as Curtice pointed out - turning smiles into frowns - the Greens now have their work cut out for them under a new and much more popular prime minister.

Polling shows support for the Greens has plummeted in the past few months.

Andy Burnham has taken steps to address key grievances that led Labour voters to switch to the Greens under Starmer.

So far, the most significant has been the Labour government's sanctions on Israeli settlements.

NAZA: Israeli embassies in UK and US promote rival documentary to challenge Gaza genocide allegations
Read More »

It is fair to assume these sanctions were partially influenced by the Greens. Polling after the local elections showed around two-thirds of voters who abandoned Labour for the Greens cited Labour's policy on Israel and Gaza as a reason.

Polanski, 43, is clearly keen to maintain the Green Party as a force shaping political discourse on Israel and Palestine. 

Two days before the conference began, he told me the British government should defy Israel's order to close the British Consulate in East Jerusalem. The deadline to close the mission is next week.

"East Jerusalem is illegally occupied Palestinian territory, and Israel has no sovereignty over it," Polanski said.

"Britain's recognition that the occupation is illegal means nothing if, whenever Israel attempts to exercise sovereign control over occupied Palestinian territory, our government simply complies."

The Green Party leader pointed out that the "consulate is also a vital diplomatic link between Britain and Palestinians in Jerusalem, the West Bank and Gaza.

"If the government means what it says about the occupied Palestinian territories," he argued, "it must put that position into practice."

'A stain and a shame on this country's reputation'

Polanski returned to the topic of Palestine in his conference speech to cheers and chants of "free, free Palestine".

He called for the government to lift its ban on the direct action group Palestine Action, and referenced the recent Labour Party conference where dozens of protesters were arrested for expressing support for the proscribed group.

"The sight of pensioners being put in handcuffs and bundled into police vans for holding up cardboard signs," Polanski said, "has been a stain and a shame on this country's reputation for far too long."

The issue of Israel's genocide in Gaza and settlements in the occupied West Bank were a major theme throughout the conference, at which there were several (all well-attended) fringe events on Palestine.

'Zionism is resulting in ethnic cleansing, in the belief that one group of people is superior to another'

 - Mothin Ali, Green Party co-deputy leader

At an event in the main auditorium on Saturday, attendees chanted "from the river to the sea, Palestine will be free" and applauded a call for "the end of the state of Israel as we know it" from the South African Jewish politician and writer Andrew Feinstein.

National media coverage of the conference was dominated by a motion to declare Zionism a form of racism, which members voted on and made official party policy on Sunday.

1,022 members voted for the motion while 813 voted against it.

The Greens are now the first major party in the country to recognise Zionism as a form of racism - and to back a single democratic Palestinian state with equal rights for all ethnic and religious groups, rather than a two-state solution. 

The motion dominated internal conversation throughout the conference and proved highly contentious.

Ali told me hours before the vote that he was strongly in favour of the motion, unlike the Green MPs Carla Denyer and Adrian Ramsay, who criticised it.

"As defined in the motion," Ali said, "Zionism is an ethno-nationalist state. Zionism is resulting in ethnic cleansing, in the belief that one group of people is superior to another."

He added: "Now I'm a committed anti-racist. I got involved in politics through the anti-racist and anti-war movement. And since then, I've got a real understanding of what racism looks like, whether it's structural, whether it's personal.

"The belief that one group of people is superior to another, I just can't accept that."

'We've always led on this subject'

Ali believed the motion would shift political discourse in Britain. "In 2024 the Green Party recognised the genocide that was taking place in Gaza, before any other major political party," he said.

"So we've always led on this subject, we've led on the subject of human rights, regardless of where it is. We're bringing other political parties with us. We're encouraging the debate to happen in society."

Before the start of the conference, it was widely reported that Jewish members of the Green Party who belong to synagogues that identified as Zionist could face internal disciplinary procedures.

I met Lubna Speitan, a British Palestinian and the lead author of the motion, on Saturday. She rubbished those claims, explaining that the motion is an "E-Motion," meaning it concerned external matters and had no bearing on internal processes. 

"We've made explicitly clear in the motion that not all Jews are Zionist and not all Zionists are Jewish," she said.

The motion was endorsed by prominent Holocaust survivor and activist Stephen Kapos, who said he believed that "Zionism both as an ideology and practice is harmful and has no legitimacy and must be rejected."

But the Jewish Greens group didn't take an official stance on the motion, saying its own members were divided on the issue.

Polanski, who is Jewish himself, said last month the motion needed to be amended to say "very clearly and explicitly that this motion safeguards Jewish people.

"And what it means by that is if someone stands against the occupation, stands against apartheid, stands against the genocide, but happens to be a member of a synagogue that calls itself a Zionist synagogue, they should not be treated any differently within the Green Party."

Ali told me on Sunday morning he agreed with this.

"It's absolutely right that E-Motions don't affect internal disciplinary procedures. But if Jewish members feel like they need an additional level of reassurance, then I think they're right to ask for that.

"All members should feel safe in this party. Not that the motion should make them feel unsafe, but if they want an additional level of reassurance, I welcome that."

The amendment, however, was defeated in a vote by members. Polanski and Ali are clearly not entirely in tune with what a significant number of Green activists believe.

Party spokespeople would not say whether Polanski would support the motion without amendments.

After the vote, the five Green MPs published a joint statement saying: "We will never tolerate any form of discrimination or harassment".

They avoided either welcoming or denouncing the vote, saying that "there is no conflict between supporting the rights of Palestinians and the rights of Jewish people."

Israel supporters hound Green members

One Green member and campaigner told me he agreed with the motion "in principle," but was unsure whether it was politically intelligent. Another member said "it won't help us on the doorsteps” to talk about ideologies and definitions.

A fierce protest erupted on the narrow street outside the Green Party conference venue in Brighton on Saturday, with dozens of pro-Israel demonstrators shouting at Green Party members as they entered the conference.

The protesters could be heard chanting "terrorist supporters off our streets" as others sang "there's no Palestine, there is no Palestine."

Some held up signs saying: "Stand up to racist Greens," "Anti Zionism = terrorism" and "More trees less Hamas". Numerous others waved Israeli flags.

A few waved a Union Jack and one man, who said he was an Indian Jew, waved a combined Israeli and Indian flag. When I politely asked him why, he accused me of being Pakistani (I am not). Eventually he explained that India and Israel are close allies in numerous ways.

Another protester, a middle-aged white man, claimed the Green Party was antisemitic.

He described Polanski as a "self-hating Jew," a derogatory term often used to disparage Jewish critics of the Israeli government.

"I'm not a Jew, I'm a Christian," he added. "I'm a Christian. We did the Holocaust." Now, he said, Jewish people were being persecuted "by Islam".

A woman who said she was French danced enthusiastically and described the Green Party as supporters of Hamas.

A group of counter-protesters, most of them Green Party members, held their own demonstration nearby.

The two sides were separated by police officers, and both were peaceful with neither side seriously confronting the other.

Some of the counter-protestors waved Palestinian flags and chanted anti-genocide slogans, while a group could be seen holding a banner reading "Jews against Zionism".

A young counter-protester named Ori, who said he was Jewish, told MEE: "We're here to support the ‘Zionism is Racism' motion. I think it will be a good thing for there to be a mainstream political party in parliament that says Zionism is racism, and that can hopefully lead to sanctions against Israel."

'Live and let live'

The conference wasn't all about controversy.

For his speech to members on Saturday, Ali danced onto the stage accompanied by a man playing a dhol (South Asian drum), to audience cheers. He embraced Rachel Millward, his co-deputy leader. 

Artificial intelligence was a prominent theme at the conference. In her speech, Millward warned that “our new oligarchical overlords would lock us into separate digital worlds flooded with AI slop and misinformation.

"A 24/7 diet of distraction and lies, hyper-scale data centres that guzzle energy to make a mockery of climate progress," she said.

'You don't have to become your neighbour. You don't have to worship like them. You don't have to vote like them. ...But you do have to recognise their equal right to exist and to belong'

- Mothin Ali, Green Party deputy leader

It was a distinctly Green message: "We don't want your post-human reality. We want this world, the soil between our toes, the trees that give us shelter and shade, the food we grow with our own hands that tastes of the ground it comes from."

Ali's speech also focused on youth unemployment and the party's plan to end it. But he also addressed issues of polarisation and division.

"The question is whether we can build a country confident enough to live with difference, to protect everyone's equal right to belong and to make diversity work for us all," Ali said, making the argument for a "live and let live" multiculturalism.

"You don't have to become your neighbour. You don't have to worship like them. You don't have to vote like them. You don't even have to agree with them.

"But you do have to recognise their equal right to exist and to belong."

He added: "Live and let live doesn't mean retreating into our separate corners. Britain has to have a conversation with itself. We have to speak to people we disagree with.

"We have to listen seriously to genuine concerns about immigration, housing, public services and security. And we need to distinguish between legitimate political arguments and the denigration of whole communities."

Polanski's own speech had focused on everyday issues faced by working people. 

It was suffused with pro-family, pro-home ownership rhetoric: "Young families are being forced to choose between moving out of the cities of the places they love, or giving up on their dreams of having a family altogether," he lamented.

Polanski argued that "building the life we want for ourselves and our kids starts with having a home of our own," saying more Green councils would mean "more homes being built, more people getting their foot on the housing ladder for the very first time, more families having that incredible feeling of putting a key in the door for the first time of their very first home."

He urged the Labour government to "put in place a three-year emergency brake on private rents." So far, Labour has ruled out rent controls.

The crucial by-election

The Green Party leader was shuttled out of the conference shortly after delivering his speech to return to London to campaign: he is the party's parliamentary candidate in a by-election in London's Holborn and St Pancras in less than a week.

This was also a hot topic among members over the weekend. A significant number had been campaigning in the seat over the past few weeks and were planning to do so in the next few days. 

Very few people said they were confident Polanski will win. All agreed it was a tall order to overturn a historic Labour majority during Burnham’s honeymoon period. Ali told me he was "quietly optimistic". 

The Green Party has been accused of sectarianism. This is why that's wrong
Read More »

Away from the main auditorium, many members spent the weekend in small rooms around the venue discussing local political strategy.

At an event about winning over Muslim voters - attended mainly by non-Muslim members - Green councillor and campaigner Asma Alam explained how she had helped Hannah Spencer win election in Gorton and Denton in February. 

This involved engagement with local Muslims and community groups, visits to mosques and even campaign videos in foreign languages. 

The Greens have been accused by their political opponents of "sectarianism" over their explicit attempts to court Muslim voters.

But what Green campaigners described here sounded more like conventional electioneering: attempting to understand voters and their concerns and to seriously engage with them.

Chris Williams, a campaigner in Leicester, discussed his experience in helping Aasiya Bora become a councillor earlier this year. 

"You often hear rumors like, 'oh, that mosque committee is endorsing Labour', or another is voting Green," Williams said.

But when people come out of the mosque, "some are saying 'no, I'm sticking with Labour', some are saying 'no, I'm going with the independent', some are saying 'no, I'm going with you'."

"The evidence that we got was that people are making their own minds up," he said.

"When you're talking to Muslim voters, and also voters who are affiliated to other religious communities, you're not talking about a bloc vote. You're talking about individual minds."

What if Polanski loses?

If Polanski, who sits on the London Assembly but has never been an MP, fails to beat Labour in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election, it will strike a massive blow to his party's image among voters - and therefore to its potential future success.

A loss could also damage Polanski's stature within the party itself.

The "Zionism is Racism" motion makes it clear that the leader is not always driving the party's agenda. This is because of its proudly democratic nature: in no other major party can ordinary members decide official policy through voting at the annual conference.

'Through our sustained pressure – and our historic wins – we have held the worst instincts of the Labour government in check'

 - Zack Polanski, Green Party leader 

This is also what energises Green members and makes so many of them heavily engaged in local politics: a sense that this is their party and they get a strong say and what it does and stands for.

It is highly possible, of course, that Polanski emerges from the by-election in a strong position in the party. 

If Holborn and St Pancras is a close challenge and Polanski comes within a few thousand votes of beating Labour, Green members will likely see this as heartening: even in difficult conditions, in a historic Labour seat and with a new prime minister, the Greens can give Labour a run for their money.

But if Polanski actually wins, it will prove the Greens still have enormous momentum. It will send Labour the message that this volatile period isn't over and even their London seats are not safe. 

With Polanski as an MP, the Greens could assert themselves as a powerful bloc in parliament influencing day-to-day political discourse.

"Vote Green and watch Labour move," Polanski declared in his leader’s speech.

"Through our sustained pressure - and our historic wins - we have held the worst instincts of the Labour government in check. And we have started to move them in the right direction."

Ali told me on Sunday: "We had a new leadership elected a year ago, and look what we’ve managed to achieve.

"That’s just the start," he said confidently. "What we can continue to do is make sure that we’re holding the government to account."

Ali added that if the Greens "are continuously providing better alternatives, the Labour government is going to have to take notice.

"And if they don't, then we're waiting to sweep up their votes."

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Toilet seats, toys and hair clips: The strangest items Israel still barred from Gaza
item.description:
Toilet seats, toys and hair clips: The strangest items Israel still barred from Gaza

Submitted by Maha Hussaini on Fri, 10/02/2026 - 10:51
A year after the ceasefire, Palestinians still struggle to find everyday items as restrictions keep basic and non-essential goods off the market
Palestinians go about their daily lives amid rainfall in Gaza City on 1 October 2026 (Mohammed M Skaik/JNA Press via Reuters)
Off

A toilet seat is all that stands between Dima Awad and moving out of her makeshift tent before winter.

The 48-year-old Palestinian mother has rented a small garage in western Gaza City and has already moved most of her belongings there.

But she cannot move in until she finds a toilet seat, something that has become increasingly difficult to find in Gaza. 

The basic item is among a range of essential goods that Israel continues to prevent from entering the besieged enclave.

“I paid the rent around 10 days ago, and I’ve been looking for a proper toilet at an affordable price for about two weeks now,” said Awad, who now lives with her only son after being separated from her husband, who travelled for treatment during the genocide.

“Of course, there is no way to find a new toilet seat at an affordable price right now. The second-hand ones are also unsuitable and still expensive.”

Due to their scarcity, toilet seats in Gaza now cost between 1,500 and 2,000 shekels ($486-648).

“I have done everything possible to move from my tent so that we wouldn’t get soaked by rainwater like we did last year. But the garage I found doesn’t have a toilet, so we have to build our own,” Awad told Middle East Eye.

“I consider the garage rent affordable after all the other unaffordable apartments I tried to rent. It costs around 600 shekels ($194) a month. But now I have to find a toilet that costs twice as much as the rent.”

A ghost list of barred items

Following the imposition of its blockade on the Gaza Strip in 2007, Israel barred or restricted the entry of numerous items, classifying them as “dual-use” goods that could potentially be used for military purposes.

These included construction materials, water and sewage pumps, electrical equipment, generators, medical equipment, wheelchairs, crutches and other items needed for basic civilian life.

In the first two years of the genocide that began in October 2023, Israel sealed Gaza’s crossings and severely restricted the entry of commercial goods and humanitarian aid, including food, medicine, fuel and other essential supplies.

Under the October 2025 ceasefire agreement, Israel was required to lift its restrictions and facilitate the flow of international humanitarian aid into Gaza. 

'We are being left without either the essentials or the non-essentials'

- Imad Sersawi, Palestinian father 

Yet, nearly a year later, vast restrictions remain, including on medicine, shelter, reconstruction materials, and other essential and non-essential items.

A range of everyday civilian and humanitarian items continue to be denied entry under what aid workers have described as a “ghost list”.

The restrictions do not stop at goods with obvious humanitarian or reconstruction uses. They extend to seemingly mundane everyday items such as batteries, lighters and children’s toys.

“I have a lighter that the entire camp borrows whenever they need to light a fire for cooking,” said Imad Sersawi, a 45-year-old Palestinian displaced from the Shujaiya neighbourhood.

“Today, whoever has a lighter is considered rich because a single lighter costs 90 shekels ($29),” he added.

“You wouldn’t even find it easily in the markets because they haven’t been allowed in months.”

Disappearing items

The father of five said more and more items are disappearing from Gaza’s markets, making everyday life increasingly uncertain.

“One day you find something; the next day it’s banned and disappears for God knows how long. Some things haven’t been allowed in for years,” he said.

“For example, I haven’t bought any toys for my children since the beginning of the genocide. Before the ceasefire agreement, they used to cry and ask for toys, and I would scold them for not understanding the situation and asking for unavailable things,” he explained.

“I used to tell them that once the war was over, I would buy them toys.” 

One year after Gaza ceasefire, killing and displacement of Palestinians persist
Read More »

But even after the ceasefire agreement, Israel continued to bar toys from entering Gaza.

Today, toy shops are selling whatever remains from before the war at exorbitant prices.

“I cannot buy them a small rubber ball for 100 shekels [$32]. That amount would feed the entire family for two days,” Sersawi continued.

“People outside Gaza might say that basic necessities are missing and that we are focusing on these secondary things. But the fact is that we are being left without either the essentials or the non-essentials.”

The system governing these restrictions remains opaque.

Israel has not published a comprehensive, updated list of dual-use items since 2017, while hundreds of items have been added to the restrictions without being publicly listed.

In practice, aid organisations and traders have had to navigate a system in which goods can be rejected because they fall outside the humanitarian category or are deemed “dual-use”.

‘Making the simplest things a struggle’

Everyday objects that would normally be taken for granted have also become difficult to find.

Baidaa Othman, a Palestinian journalist, had to travel between two governorates to find a hair claw clip, eventually paying around 10 times its original price.

“Now it’s not just about being able to get the basic necessities. It has reached a point where, when you want to buy something very simple, you have to go to extraordinary lengths to find it,” Othman told MEE.

“Even the simplest things as basic as a hair clip have become difficult to find. On top of all the basic necessities that are unavailable in Gaza, now the everyday things that no one would normally think twice about have become unavailable.”

In an Instagram video, Sojood Hasan, a Palestinian physiotherapist in Gaza, highlighted how restrictions on hair clips reflect a wider loss of everyday choices for women in the Strip.

“No one collapses because a hair clip is missing. But the feeling that your life is not in your hands can wear you down,” the young woman said.

'This is not random; it is a policy of making even the simplest things a struggle for Gazans'

- Baidaa Othman, Palestinian journalist

For Othman, who is originally from Gaza City and remains displaced in Deir al-Balah in central Gaza after her home was destroyed, the need for such an ordinary item is inseparable from the daily realities of displacement.

“On top of the displacement and all the hardships we face, including having to cook with firewood, it’s only natural for women to want to put their hair up to keep it off their faces and necks in the heat. So it’s not a secondary item any more,” she said.

A clip that once cost around four shekels ($1.3) cost her 45 shekels ($14.5). 

“The Israeli occupation knows exactly what it is doing,” Othman said. 

“This is not random; it is a policy of making even the simplest things a struggle for Gazans.”

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Is Ethiopia repeating its oldest mistake?
item.description:
Is Ethiopia repeating its oldest mistake?

Submitted by Yunus Turhan on Thu, 10/01/2026 - 16:33
When past leaders have tried to govern from a single centre, the country's peripheries have united in opposition
Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed attends a meeting in Moscow, Russia, on 25 September 2025 (Evgenia Novozhenina/AFP)
On

Ethiopia’s history has come back to haunt it. 

Late last month, seven armed groups - among them the Fano militia in Amhara, the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) and the Oromo Liberation Army - announced the formation of the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival, and vowed to remove Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed. 

Within days, Tigrayan forces had seized the airports in Mekelle, Axum and Shire, and opened fronts in Afar and Amhara. By 25 September, phone and internet lines in Tigray were cut. This time it was the TPLF, not Addis Ababa, that ordered the blackout.

Most commentary reads the new conflict as the collapse of the Pretoria agreement, a 2022 peace deal to end two years of war. But the story is much older than the Pretoria process and Abiy himself.

For nearly two centuries, Ethiopian politics has swung between a centre that wants to command, and regions that insist on ruling themselves. Each time the pendulum has pushed hard towards the centre, the peripheries have found a way to unite against it.

After the Zemane Mesafint (“Era of the Princes”) in the 18th and 19th centuries, when regional lords ran their own affairs, Tewodros II tried to rebuild the empire by the sword. The provinces revolted one after another, and in 1868, he died at Magdala, his army reduced to remnants.

Similarly, former emperor Haile Selassie’s 1962 dissolution of the Eritrean federation turned a small insurgency into a 30-year war. The Derg regime pushed centralisation to its limits, and fell in 1991 to a coalition of ethno-regional groups, the Ethiopian People’s Revolutionary Democratic Front (EPRDF). 

The 1995 constitution swung back by creating ethnic federalism and, in Article 39, even a right to secession. Yet the EPRDF ran that system through party discipline from Addis Ababa, so self-rule stayed largely on paper. 

In short, Ethiopia’s state structure has swung between centralisation and decentralisation over 170 years.

Tensions unresolved

Abiy assumed power in 2018 by preaching Medemer, an approach of reconciliation and national unity in the face of ethnic divisions. But it quickly began to unravel in 2019, when he dissolved the EPRDF to form his Prosperity Party. 

Tensions long kept under wraps soon boiled over, and to contain them, Abiy returned to the tools of his predecessors: mass arrests of suspected opponents, and new restrictions on the media.

War with the TPLF followed in 2020, fought alongside forces from Eritrea and Amhara. After the Pretoria agreement in 2022, Abiy disbanded the regional special forces, which pushed the Fano militia into open revolt. The status of Welkait and Raya, claimed by both Amhara and Tigray, was left unresolved after Pretoria, so both sides felt cheated.

The coalition now marching against Abiy is largely made up of the forces with which he won the last war

What made such an unlikely alliance possible? The answer lies less with the rebels than with the centre’s own choices. Each centralising step cost Abiy a partner. 

Eritrea, kept away from the Pretoria table, watched its old enemy survive, and then heard Addis Ababa speak of a Red Sea port in terms Asmara read as a claim on Assab. The special forces decision did the same to Amhara. 

In short, the coalition now marching against Abiy is largely made up of the forces with which he won the last war. 

Can the new alliance muster the capacity to challenge Abiy’s rule? This is not likely, at least for the time being. The alliance has named no joint military commander, and unlike 1991, it has no dominant force able to march on the capital. 

Abiy has a drone fleet the Derg never had, along with a fresh mandate from the public, as his party won 438 of the 501 contested seats in parliament (nearly 90 percent) this past June. But some groups have rejected the results, and voting did not take place in Tigray, which comprises 38 constituencies.

The road ahead

Three paths seem possible from here for Abiy. In the first, he peels Amhara away with concessions over Welkait, while the TPLF’s seizure of airports enables him to present it as the aggressor. The price is that any Welkait deal with Fano locks Tigray into permanent war, so dividing the alliance on one front deepens the other. 

In the second, the war settles into a stalemate: the centre holds the cities and the skies, armed movements hold the countryside, and Ethiopia drifts towards a de facto confederation run by men with guns - a Zemene Mesafint by other means. 

The third is the most dangerous. Abiy has a record of seeking a unifying cause abroad when pressed at home; once it was the Renaissance Dam (where Egypt is a factor), and today it is access to the sea. This time, a move towards Assab would turn a civil war into a war with Eritrea, and pull in every regional power watching.

The regional map explains why that third path cannot be dismissed. The fault lines of Sudan’s war now run through Ethiopia. On one side sits the UAE, Abiy’s main supporter since 2018, whose drones are widely credited with turning the last war, and which analysts accuse of routing arms through Ethiopia to Sudan’s Rapid Support Forces.

Gold, arms and mercenaries: On UAE's shadowy networks in Sudan
Read More »

 Israel’s recognition of Somaliland in December 2025, widely seen as brokered by Abu Dhabi, and President Isaac Herzog’s visit to Addis Ababa in February tied Ethiopia’s hunger for the sea to Emirati-Israeli designs for the Red Sea. 

On the other side, Egypt, which regards the Renaissance Dam as a threat to its survival, has built an axis with Eritrea and Somalia, and backs Sudan’s army, with Saudi Arabia reportedly drawing closer to Asmara. 

A simultaneous rift with Egypt and Eritrea would carry a heavy price for Abiy Ahmed's government, since Addis Ababa would then face hostile fault lines to both its north and its east.

Cairo has pledged troops to the African Union mission in Somalia, and Eritrea has already placed itself at the heart of the dispute by severing diplomatic relations with Ethiopia altogether.

Hemmed in on both flanks, Ethiopia would depend almost entirely on Djibouti, which already handles close to 90 percent of its trade.

For Ahmed, a war on several fronts would revive what Otto von Bismarck called his "cauchemar des coalitions", the "nightmare of coalitions" in which France and Russia might join forces and drag Germany into a two-front war.

Fighting at home while quarrelling abroad would be the worst of all scenarios for Addis Ababa, once the military costs, the strain on debt relief and the human toll are counted together.

For Cairo, an Ethiopia tied down at home is leverage on the Nile. For Abu Dhabi, a collapsing Ethiopia would mean losing its most valuable partner on the mainland. Both camps thus have reasons to feed the war, yet neither has much interest in a clear winner. That is how civil wars become proxy wars. 

This is where Turkey matters. It brokered the Ankara Declaration between Ethiopia and Somalia in December 2024, while holding its largest overseas base in Mogadishu, and has mended ties with both Cairo and Abu Dhabi in recent years. This gives Ankara a rare ability to speak to both camps. As his room at home narrows, Abiy may well knock on Ankara’s door again.

Ethiopia’s prognosis therefore hinges on Abiy’s next move: whether he adopts collaborative, win-win strategies towards his opponents, or clings to a zero-sum game. In making that choice, he would do well to look back, for Ethiopian history is clear on one point: the state has held when power was bargained with the regions, and it has cracked whenever power was imposed on them. 

The reason is simple. Once power has been devolved to the peripheries, it can rarely be recentralised without resistance - and this is precisely the lesson Abiy must now come to terms with.

The National Weather Service in the US has issued extreme heat warnings for parts of southern California, including Los Angeles, until Thursday, as temperatures are expected to hit the high 30s celsius. Burbank, a suburb north of Los Angeles, recorded 39C on Saturday, a few degrees shy of the October record for the region set in 1987. A persistent area of high pressure will remain in place this week, leading to further hazardous hot weather and increased fire risk.

Parts of Indonesia are in the midst of an extreme wildfire season, which has peaked over the past month. Western Kalimantan (Borneo) and southern Sumatra have been particularly badly affected. The lack of rainfall has dried the usually water-logged tropical soils, meaning that fires have been able to spread quickly, above and below the surface. Indonesia’s soils are also extremely rich in peat, meaning that the smoke produced from the fires contain higher levels of toxic gases such as sulphur dioxide and carbon monoxide. Cities in surrounding areas and as far as Malaysia and Singapore have experienced reduced air quality in recent weeks as a result. Drought and wildfires are more common in this part of the world during El Niño events owing to suppressed thunderstorm activity.

item.description:
Israel bans Zack Polanski after Green Party backs 'Zionism is racism' motion

Submitted by MEE staff on Mon, 10/05/2026 - 10:04
Israel's foreign ministry accuses Green Party of legitimising 'destruction of the state of Israel'
Zack Polanski (right), poses for a photo in London on 12 September, ahead of the Holborn and St Pancras by-election (AFP/Toby Shepheard)
Off

Israel has banned Green Party leader Zack Polanski from entering the country after the party approved a motion at its conference declaring "Zionism is racism".

In a statement on Sunday, Israel accused the Green Party of England and Wales of legitimising "the destruction of the State of Israel".

Israel’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said the resolution, which also advocates for a one-state solution in historic Palestine, “constitutes a clear antisemitic text according to the IHRA definition, as it denies the Jewish people’s right to self-determination”.

“Therefore, as a first step, foreign minister Gideon Sa’ar has decided this evening to declare Green Party leader Zack Polanski barred from entering Israel,” it said.

According to Israel's Law of Return, persons with at least one Jewish grandparent, and their spouses, have a legal right to enter, reside in, and acquire citizenship of, the State of Israel.

However, Israel has occasionally banned certain Jewish people from entering the country if it deems them a security risk, or they question Israel's legitimacy. In practice, this has often meant political opponents of the state.

The vote by party members on Sunday makes the Green Party the first major party in the UK to recognise Zionism as a form of racism - and to back a single democratic Palestinian state with equal rights for all ethnic and religious groups, rather than a two-state solution. 

At the conference in Brighton this weekend, 1,022 members voted for the motion while 813 voted against it.

Co-deputy leader Mothin Ali told Middle East Eye on Sunday that he was strongly in favour of the motion, unlike Green MPs Carla Denyer and Adrian Ramsay, who criticised it.

'We're waiting to sweep up their votes': Three days inside the Green Party conference
Read More »

"As defined in the motion," Ali said, "Zionism is an ethno-nationalist state. Zionism is resulting in ethnic cleansing, in the belief that one group of people is superior to another."

Green members voted against an amendment to the motion saying it "shall not be used to pressure, proscribe or discipline members based on affiliation with Jewish community institutions, such as synagogues, community centres or denominational groups, that describe themselves as Zionist or used to discipline or sanction Jewish members for expressing views that would be non sanctionable if expressed by non Jewish members (such as support for a binational state, or two state solution)."

But members voted for an amendment supporting the "inalienable right to self-determination" for Palestinians, party insiders told MEE.

Party spokespeople on Sunday morning would not say whether Polanski would support the motion without amendments.

After the vote, the five Green MPs published a joint statement saying: "We will never tolerate any form of discrimination or harassment".

They added that "there is no conflict between supporting the rights of Palestinians and the rights of Jewish people."

Yemen's Saudi-backed forces claim key gains around Bab al-Mandab strait

Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces said on Monday that they had seized key positions on the Bab al-Mandab strait from the Houthis.

Three military sources and one government source told Reuters their forces had taken large parts of Dhubab district, which overlooks the strategically vital strait, and that they were asserting full control over the area with heavy air support from a Saudi-led coalition.

The forces are fighting to reverse significant advances made by the Iran-aligned Houthis and to drive them from the Bab al-Mandab.

Houthi-aligned media had earlier denied that government forces had made advances in the area.
